explanations.answer: A help that is always there
explanations.explanation: The song says God is “…an ever-present help in times of trouble.” Ever-present means He's already in the room. Nobody has to go find Him. That's like the friend who's standing in your kitchen before you even finish yelling about the smoke.

explanations.answer: A help that comes when we call
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but that's not the word the song picks. It says God is “…an ever-present help in times of trouble.” That help isn't waiting on a phone call. It's already there. Ever-present means you never have to wonder if He's on His way.

explanations.answer: A help that comes when trouble ends
explanations.explanation: I get why that sounds nice, but the song puts His help right inside the trouble. It says He is “…an ever-present help in times of trouble.” In times of trouble, not after them. Imagine a firefighter who shows up once the fire is out and the kitchen's already cold. That's not the help this song is singing about.

Right there in verse 2: “Therefore we will not fear…” That word "therefore" ties it straight back to God being their refuge and strength. The earth can be transformed and the mountains can topple, and they still sing it. I'd be hiding under my apron at the first rumble, so this is some serious steadiness.
Funny thing, they're singing the whole time. This is a song, and it keeps right on going through the roaring seas. What they say they will not do is fear. Singing is how they say it.

The song doesn't say anything about not resting here. It says, “Therefore we will not fear…” The word "therefore" points back to God being their refuge and strength. That's why they can sing about toppling mountains without panicking.

Verse 4 says there is “…a river whose streams delight the city of God.” After all that roaring and foaming, this river is the calm after the noise. The song also says it's the holy place where the Most High dwells. Streams that make a whole city glad. I'd stand there with my hat off, and I never take my hat off.
Danger fits the waters in verse 3, the ones that roar and foam. But verse 4 turns a corner. The river's streams “…delight the city of God.” Same song, very different water.

The sea before it sounds scary, so I see why sorrow came to mind. But the song says the streams of this river “…delight the city of God.” It's a happy river, friend. The song goes from roaring waters to gladness in one breath.

Mountains topple in verse 2, so I see why this one tripped you up. But verse 5 says it the other way: “God is within her; she will not be moved.” The city of God stays put because God is within her. Mountains move, and she doesn't.

Yes, friend. Mountains topple in verse 2, but verse 5 says, “God is within her; she will not be moved.” The mountains move, and the city of God doesn't. The song gives the reason right there: God is within her.

Verse 5 says, “God will help her when morning dawns.” Morning is when the dark is done and the light comes in. I know a thing or two about dark places, and I can tell you the first light is a welcome sight. The song puts God's help right there at dawn.

The sea does roar and foam back in verse 3, but the song never ties God's help to it calming down. Verse 5 says, “God will help her when morning dawns.” Dawn is the time it names. The calm-sea part is a nice thought, just not what the song says.
Nations show up in the song, but not at this line. Verse 5 says, “God will help her when morning dawns.” It's the dawn that carries the promise. Nothing here says the help waits on anybody bowing.

Verse 6 says, “Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice.” Look at who's doing the big thing there. Nations rage and kingdoms crumble, but the earth melts when God lifts His voice. I lift my voice and the dough doesn't even flinch.

The song does say it, friend. Verse 6 reads, “Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice.” The earth melting is tied to His voice. All the raging nations are loud, but His voice is the one that makes the earth melt.

Verse 7 says, “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.” With us. Right after the nations rage and the earth melts, that's the line the singers land on. It's the same ever-present help from verse 1, just sung louder.
The song never says He's far off. Verse 7 says, “The LORD of Hosts is with us…” With us, not above us at a distance. After all that raging and melting, that's the line they sing.

explanations.answer: He is still on His way
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, friend, but verse 7 says, “The LORD of Hosts is with us…” That's present tense, so He isn't on His way. He's already with them. Nobody here is checking the window for His arrival.
Verse 8 says, “Come, see the works of the LORD…” The song is waving everybody over to look at what God has done. It doesn't point at buildings or loot. It points at Him and His works.

The song does talk about a city, the city of God in verse 4. But the invitation in verse 8 is, “Come, see the works of the LORD…” That's what we're called to look at. Walls don't come up in this song at all.
Treasures and temples don't show up in this song, friend. The invitation in verse 8 is, “Come, see the works of the LORD…” The works of the LORD are what the song wants us looking at.

Verse 8 says the works of the LORD include one “…who brings devastation upon the earth.” That isn't quiet or gentle. Verse 9 goes on to say that He breaks the bow and shatters the spear. So the song shows works with real force in them.

Right, and the song says so itself. Verse 8 calls Him the one “…who brings devastation upon the earth.” Then verse 9 says He breaks the bow and shatters the spear. Those are strong works, not soft ones.

Verse 9 says, “He makes wars to cease throughout the earth…” Bows broken, spears shattered, shields burned. It all goes with wars coming to an end. A whole pile of broken weapons is a pretty clear sign that the fighting is done.
Verse 9 says it covers “…throughout the earth.” That's not one town or one border. He makes wars cease everywhere. I can barely get one kitchen to quiet down.
The sea did roar back in verse 3, so storms feel close. But verse 9 says, “He makes wars to cease throughout the earth…” Wars are what stop. Broken bows and burned shields fit that, not weather.

The city of God does show up earlier, in verse 4, so I see why it came to mind. But verse 9 says, “He makes wars to cease throughout the earth…” Throughout the earth is much bigger than one city. The song is looking at the whole world here.

Roaring waters came up in verse 3, so floods make sense as a guess. But in verse 9 what ceases is wars. It says He makes them cease “…throughout the earth.” Bows, spears and shields all point to the end of war.

Verse 10 says, “Be still and know that I am God…” Here God Himself is speaking, and what He asks us to know is who He is. After all that raging and melting, that's the thing to hold onto. It's good news, friend.
The seas roared back in verse 3, so I see the link. But God's words in verse 10 are, “Be still and know that I am God…” What He asks us to know is that He is God. The seas aren't part of that line.
Mountains toppled earlier in the song, so it's an easy guess. But in verse 10 God says, “Be still and know that I am God…” The thing to know is who He is, not what the mountains will do.

In verse 10, God says, “…I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth.” Nations were raging back in verse 6, and here God says He will be exalted among them. The nations and the whole earth are both named.

Angels don't come up in this song, friend. God says in verse 10, “…I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth.” The nations are the ones named. It's a wide, whole-earth kind of promise.

Priests aren't in this song. In verse 10, God says, “…I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth.” The nations are the ones He names. That's a lot bigger room than any one group.
